body.text: Eyre Peninsula locals count losses after strong winds topple power towers
In short:
Farmers and local businesses are assessing the damage caused by a "rare" storm supercell that toppled transmission towers and cut power to the Eyre Peninsula.
Works are underway to restore power to the region.
What's next?
The SA premier says there will be an "appropriate examination" of why ElectraNet's infrastructure failed under the circumstances.
Shed doors were blown off and crops wiped out during a "rare" storm supercell that flattened major electricity transmission towers on South Australia's Eyre Peninsula.
Locals are surveying the damage caused by severe winds which tore across the region, cutting power to about 24,000 properties at 3pm on Thursday.
Wharminda resident Sarah Prime stood outside her home watching the wild weather sweep over her paddocks, a scene she described like something out of a Ridley Scott movie.
"All of a sudden, everything in the backyard was just lifting up and whizzing around, and I actually went and got our dog — I thought she was going to blow away," she said.
With November prime harvest time for many across the state, the timing was not welcomed.
"There are some areas that are completely flattened, and you know, bits of the crop are hanging in trees or over the power lines and things like that," Ms Prime said.
"There are parts that will be affected but not damaged as badly, and then there'll be other parts that aren't touched at all."
Sarah's brother-in-law Jarrod Prime was working in his shed when the wind ripped its 600-kilogram door off its hinges.
"I just started running for my life up at the other end of the shed," he said.
"It was a pretty harrowing experience, the worst I have ever felt.
"I'm very distraught with the damage, but luckily everyone is safe."
ElectraNet said the significant winds brought down two major transmission towers and damaged a third — infrastructure that was only upgraded three years ago.
Grain Producers SA chief executive Brad Perry said farmers were assessing damage and it was too early to know if the storm had impacted harvest figures this year.
"We certainly feel for those growers," he told SA Country Hour.
"It's looking like a record crop and suddenly having it on the ground is devastating," he said.
Local businesses lose thousands
Arno Bay Jetty Cafe owner Kath Tayler said her losses were already over $10,000 and could reach $20,000 depending on the weather in the coming days.
The cafe's freezers are currently unable to connect to her small generator.
"I'm too scared to open the big freezer room because I'm not sure what we're going to find," she said.
"Depending on what happens with the big freezer room … if it's [stock] just defrosted, we can still use it, we just can't obviously refreeze it.
"We also had a milk order delivery that came this morning … so that milk is still sitting out in the shop, just getting hot, so we'll lose all that as well plus what's already in the fridges."
Power progressively being restored
While a large portion of the region had their lights back on, just over 1000 properties remained without power as at 4:45pm on Friday, according to SA Power Networks's outage map.
At Friday's press conference, SA Premier Peter Malinauskas said a bypass line was being installed to connect the West Coast and Upper Eyre Peninsula "later today".
Temporary measures to bring supply back are also underway, including crane installations to "re-erect" the transmission line and temporary tower installations in the coming days.
A 20-megawatt generator located in Port Lincoln has been powering the township and lower Eyre Peninsula since Thursday night.
All residents in the area have been urged to turn off their solar panels to ensure the generator does not exceed its level of demand.
Mr Malinauskas said while it was great news the generator was working as it should, there were other risks ahead.
"We're not out of the woods yet, there is still storm events coming our way, extreme fire conditions over the course of the weekend," he said.
"The generator itself is temperamental in nature. It is in a very old piece of equipment and we should be alive to the prospect that that may fail, and that's why we continue to monitor it."
Towers were up to standard
ElectraNet executive network manager Alex Trento said the transmission towers that fell were designed to withstand up to around 170km/h wind speed.
"The design of these towers are also tested to destruction, that is to the actual design standard that they're meant to abide by,"
Mr Trento said he did not know what the wind speed was when the towers toppled but the probability of it occurring was "very rare".
When asked if there could be a reason other than strong winds that knock down the towers, Mr Trento said structural fault in the towers was "a possibility" and ElectraNet was investigating.
"At this point in time, seeing the localisation of the event, we do think that the towers have been designed and constructed effectively," he said.
ElectraNet expected an estimate of the cost of repairs to be available "in the next three to six months".
Mr Malinauskas confirmed the state government would also be reviewing what had occurred over the past 24 hours.
"There will be an appropriate examination of ElectraNet's infrastructure and why it's failed under these circumstances," he said.
